title: Motion Along a Straight Line
learning_objectives: Describe one dimensional motion in terms of position, displacement, distance, velocity, speed and acceleration.
Tell a scalar from a vector and apply that distinction to the quantities of motion.
Use the equations of constant acceleration to solve problems about motion in a straight line.
Read a motion from a position time graph and from a velocity time graph.

sections.title: Introduction to One-Dimensional Kinematics
objectives: Describe what kinematics studies and how it differs from dynamics.

misconceptions.claim: Kinematics and dynamics are two names for the same subject.
misconceptions.correction: Kinematics describes how things move, with no mention of a cause. Dynamics explains why they move, through forces.

summary: Kinematics describes motion in terms of position and time.
One dimensional motion happens along a straight line.
Kinematics comes first, because the causes of motion come later.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Displacement
objectives: Define position and displacement on a coordinate system, and tell displacement from distance.

misconceptions.claim: Distance and displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Distance is the length of the path and is never negative. Displacement is the straight line from the start to the end, and it carries a direction.

summary: Position locates an object on a coordinate system.
Displacement is the change in position, and it is a vector.
Distance is the total path length, and it is a scalar.

sections.title: Vectors, Scalars, and Coordinate Systems
objectives: Tell a scalar from a vector, and place a point on a one dimensional coordinate system.

misconceptions.claim: Speed and velocity mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is a scalar, the distance over time. Velocity is a vector, the displacement over time, and it also carries a direction.

summary: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has magnitude and direction.
Displacement and velocity are vectors. Distance and speed are scalars.
A one dimensional coordinate system is a number line with an origin and a positive direction.

sections.title: Time, Velocity, and Speed
objectives: Define average velocity and average speed, and compute them from a motion diagram.

misconceptions.claim: Average velocity tells you how fast the object is moving right now.
misconceptions.correction: Average velocity covers the whole journey. The speed at a moment is the instantaneous speed.

summary: Average velocity is displacement over time.
Average speed is distance over time.
Average speed is never smaller than the magnitude of the average velocity.

sections.title: Acceleration
objectives: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity and read it from a velocity time graph.

misconceptions.claim: An object with zero acceleration must be at rest.
misconceptions.correction: Zero acceleration means the velocity is not changing. The object may be moving at a constant velocity.

summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so it is a vector.
Positive acceleration means the velocity is increasing, negative means it is decreasing.
The sign of acceleration does not tell you the direction of the motion.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Motion Equations for Constant Acceleration in One Dimension
objectives: Use the equations of constant acceleration, and choose which one fits the question.

misconceptions.claim: The constant acceleration equations work for any motion.
misconceptions.correction: They hold only while the acceleration stays constant. If the acceleration changes, the equations do not apply.

summary: The equations relate position, velocity, acceleration and time for constant acceleration.
Each equation leaves out one of the quantities.
Choose the equation by listing what you know and what you want.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Problem-Solving Basics for One-Dimensional Kinematics
objectives: Set up a kinematics problem: draw it, list what is known, choose the equation, solve, and check.

misconceptions.claim: You can start algebra on a physics problem without knowing which quantities you have.
misconceptions.correction: List what is known and what is wanted first. Then the equation chooses itself.

summary: Draw the situation, then list what is known and what is wanted.
Choose the equation, solve, and check the signs and the units.
A sign convention applies to every quantity, not only to the answer.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Falling Objects
objectives: Model free fall as constant acceleration and read the motion off a motion diagram.

misconceptions.claim: A heavier object falls faster than a lighter one.
misconceptions.correction: Without air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration, whatever its mass. Air resistance is what separates a feather from a stone.

summary: Near the Earth's surface, free fall has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s² downward.
The acceleration is the same for every object. The velocity is not.
Air resistance makes real falls differ from the model.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Graphical Analysis of One-Dimensional Motion
objectives: Read a position time graph and a velocity time graph, and use their slopes and areas.

misconceptions.claim: The area under a velocity time graph is the distance travelled.
misconceptions.correction: The area under the curve is the displacement, because velocity is signed. Distance is the area under the speed curve, where the speed is never negative.

summary: The slope of a position time graph is the velocity.
The slope of a velocity time graph is the acceleration.
The area under a velocity time graph is the displacement.

definition.text: The study of how objects move, without asking what causes the motion.
The location of an object on a coordinate system, measured from the origin.
The change in position of an object, with direction. It is the straight line from the start to the end, not the path.
Displacement divided by the time it took, so it is a vector.
The rate at which the velocity changes with time. It is a vector.
Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected, so every object shares the same acceleration.
